--- title: "Estimate a hemodynamic response" subtitle: "Fit smooth FIR curves and inspect their uncertainty." jupyter: python3 --- A canonical HRF fixes the response shape before fitting. When the shape itself is the question, `estimate_hrf` fits condition-level curves using a smooth finite impulse response (FIR) basis. It returns an `HrfEstimate` with response curves, standard errors, intervals, and the selected smoothing penalty. This example uses simulated data so the fitted shape can be compared with the generating HRF. On a narrow screen, scroll plots horizontally to read their labels. Select a plot to open a complete view. ## Simulate two condition responses The event model generates an SPM canonical response for two alternating conditions. Condition B has twice the amplitude of condition A in the first feature. The second feature has a smaller response to both conditions. ::: {#28f7b860 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import fmrimod as fm rng = np.random.default_rng(180) events = pd.DataFrame({ "onset": np.arange(8.0, 190.0, 10.0), "condition": np.resize(["A", "B"], 19), "duration": 0.0, "run": 1, }) sampling = fm.SamplingFrame(blocklens=220, TR=1.0) generating_model = fm.event_model( "onset ~ hrf(condition, basis='spmg1')", data=events, sampling_frame=sampling, durations=0.0, block="run", ) amplitudes = np.array([[1.0, 0.7], [2.0, 1.4]]) signal = np.asarray(generating_model.design_matrix) @ amplitudes response = signal + rng.normal(scale=0.04, size=signal.shape) dataset = fm.fmri_dataset(response, tr=1.0, events=events) ``` ::: ## Fit the response shape Formula-plus-dataset calls without a numeric basis select the smooth FIR estimator. Here `k=8` sets eight free B-spline coefficients per curve, and `lam="gcv"` chooses one smoothing penalty by generalized cross-validation across the responses. The default baseline is a constant. The estimated curves are constrained to zero at the start and end of the requested span. ::: {#54bc1c17 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} hrf_fit = fm.estimate_hrf( form="onset ~ hrf(condition)", dataset=dataset, block="run", rsam=np.arange(0.0, 21.0), k=8, lam="gcv", ci_level=0.95, ) hrf_fit.curve_info ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
curve term condition
0 condition.A condition condition.A
1 condition.B condition condition.B
``` ::: ::: The estimate arrays are ordered as time × curve × feature. Use `curve_info` to identify the curves and `time` for the post-stimulus grid. ::: {#6b103e5d .cell fig-height='3.6' fig-width='9' execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.6), sharex=True, sharey=True) truth_shape = np.asarray(fm.get_hrf("spmg1")(hrf_fit.time)).reshape(-1) for curve, ax in enumerate(axes): color = ["#24786f", "#c26143"][curve] label = str(hrf_fit.curve_info.iloc[curve]["condition"]) truth_row = 0 if label.endswith("A") else 1 ax.plot(hrf_fit.time, hrf_fit.estimate[:, curve, 0], color=color, label="FIR estimate") ax.fill_between(hrf_fit.time, hrf_fit.lower[:, curve, 0], hrf_fit.upper[:, curve, 0], color=color, alpha=0.18) ax.plot(hrf_fit.time, truth_shape * amplitudes[truth_row, 0], color="#526265", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.3, label="Generating HRF") ax.axhline(0, color="#aeb8b7", linewidth=0.7) ax.set_title(f"Condition {label.rsplit('.', 1)[-1]}") ax.set_xlabel("Time after event (s)") axes[0].set_ylabel("Response amplitude") axes[1].legend(loc="upper right") fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Simulated data, feature 1. Solid curves are smooth FIR estimates; dashed curves are the generating HRFs. Shading shows 95% pointwise model intervals. These intervals do not account for model-selection uncertainty or unmodeled temporal correlation.](estimating-hrfs_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){fig-alt='Two panels comparing smooth FIR estimates for conditions A and B with the simulated SPM response in feature one. Shaded bands show model intervals. Condition B has twice the amplitude.'} ::: ::: ## Inspect the smoothing choice The selected penalty and effective degrees of freedom describe the fitted curve's flexibility. GCV chooses from the candidate grid; it does not prove that the response model or residual assumptions are appropriate for a real acquisition. ::: {#f826f75f .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} pd.Series({ "selected penalty": hrf_fit.lam, "effective degrees of freedom": hrf_fit.edf, "residual degrees of freedom": hrf_fit.df_residual, "curves": len(hrf_fit.curves), "features": len(hrf_fit.voxels), }) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` selected penalty 0.021544 effective degrees of freedom 14.205856 residual degrees of freedom 204.794144 curves 2.000000 features 2.000000 dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: For labeled output, use `hrf_fit.tidy()`. To evaluate the fitted curves on another grid within the fitted span, use `hrf_fit.predict(...)`. Matrix calls that supply `Y`, `X_trials`, and a numeric two-dimensional `basis` use the older voxel-HRF compatibility estimator; they do not return this smooth FIR result. ## Next - [HRF estimator reference](../reference/estimate_hrf.qmd) - [Smooth FIR estimator reference](../reference/estimate_hrf_fir.qmd) - [Plotting and visualization](plotting-visualization.qmd) - [Single-trial estimates](single-trial.qmd)
